newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai economic guru sees recovery ahead.
newsitem.headline: Thai economic guru sees recovery ahead.

text.p: A leading Thai economic figure said on Tuesday Bangkok's stock market will recover and that market forces will help the economy improve next year, despite the change of government after last weekend's election.

"I cannot help feeling optimistic about the prospect that we will have a recovery and a stable economy starting from 1997," said Narongchai Akrasanee, head of General Finance and Security Co Ltd, who is also an adviser to Amnuay Viravan, a caretaker deputy prime minister and foreign minister.

"We can expect the power of the market forces ... would keep Thailand in the right direction regardless of how unpopular the government is," Narongchai told a gathering of the Asia Society in Hong Kong.
Amnuay was also in Hong Kong for a Europe-East Asia summit of the World Economic Forum.

Amnuay said on Monday he was considering an offer from the winning New Aspiration Party, which is expected to form the next government as part of a coalition, to take charge of Thailand's economic policy.
Narongchai said he was not expected to be included in the next Thai cabinet, although he described himself as an insider.

He said he believed the coalition government now being formed would introduce policies that continued to promote market forces. It would press on with deregulation, accelerate the development of capital and money markets and pension funds, and would exercise fiscal restraint, he said.
He said the coalition parties would announce a detailed policy package on Monday, November 25.
"I believe they will try harder to please the business community and the international community."

Noting the slowdown in Thailand's economy after many years of rapid expansion, Narongchai said growth was returning to a "basic level" and that growth this year would be "maybe six percent", and this would become the norm for the next few years. He also forecast export growth of three to five percent for the year.

Thailand's economy in terms of gross domestic product (GDP) has grown an average of about nine percent a year over the past decade. GDP, which is officially forecast to grow by 7.8 percent for the year, is expected by most economists to rise just above six percent in 1996.
Narongchai was positive about Thailand's stock market after it fell sharply on Monday, the first day of trade after the general election.
He noted that by Monday night, a whiff of optimism was already back in the air after clear signs the coalition government being formed would install a cabinet acceptable to the business community.

He said a stock market recovery was well under way on Tuesday morning. The main SET index ended Tuesday up 21.85 points, or 2.32 percent, at 964.19, although it ended on Monday nearly six percent down.
Narongchai said that in recent times, Thailand had undergone a "coup d'etat of market forces", which had replaced a tradition of "coup d'etat by armed forces".

"The Thai economy is very much market driven ... Although we have this short-term liquidity problem, the structural adjustment will definitely take place, will continue and the Thai economy will emerge from this period of small growth stronger and more advanced."
He cautioned however that the next six weeks were crucial and much depended on how the next administration managed the liquidity crunch.
